one_liner: Rust research benchmark: Moeller-Granlund reciprocal 128-bit division vs __udivti3, native and Wasm wide-arithmetic; wins mainly with hoisted divisors.
what_it_does: A Rust binary crate (publish = false) with two drop-in-shaped sets of functions, udivrem128/udiv128/urem128 and signed sdivrem128/sdiv128/srem128, one using Rust's u128/i128 operators (the __udivti3/__umodti3 libcall) and one built from add, sub and 64x64-to-128 multiplies that lower to the Wasm wide-arithmetic proposal (i64.add128, i64.sub128, i64.mul_wide_u). Criterion runs both natively, under d8 (V8, TurboFan only) and under wasmtime (Cranelift), and scripts/report.py writes the comparison table. The README also sketches two proposed Wasm instructions, i64.recip128 (divisor normalisation plus reciprocal) and i64.divrem_recip128 (quotient and remainder from that prep), so a loop-invariant reciprocal can be hoisted.
how_it_is_fast: Division by an invariant integer via a precomputed reciprocal (Moeller and Granlund, 'Improved division by invariant integers'): a 256-entry u16 table seeds Algorithm 2's Newton steps to get floor((2^128-1)/d) - 2^64, then 2-by-1 (64-bit divisor) or 3-by-2 (full-width divisor) kernels replace the divide with a multiply-high, a multiply-low and at most two correction steps. Splitting the reciprocal (recip128) from the divide (divrem_recip128) lets a caller compute it once outside a loop, which the opaque libcall cannot do. Shortcuts return early when the divisor's high word exceeds the dividend's (quotient 0) or when the divisor is already normalised (quotient 0 or 1).
when_to_use: Designing or evaluating Wasm engine or toolchain support for 128-bit division on top of the wide-arithmetic proposal; the report and the i64.recip128 / i64.divrem_recip128 sketch are the point of the repo.

Native x86_64 code that divides many 128-bit values by one fixed divisor on a CPU where the 128/64 DIV instruction is slow (the measured machine is a Coffee Lake i9-9880H): port the 2-by-1/3-by-2 kernels and hoist recip128.
Wanting a readable, unit-tested Rust reference of Moeller-Granlund reciprocal division (500,000-case random and edge-value tests against the native operators).
when_not_to_use: One-off 128-bit divisions in Wasm: the builtin libcall is faster on V8 (reciprocal 19.6% to 33.4% slower) and about equal on wasmtime (-0.7% to +10.3%).
Production code: no LICENSE file (raw LICENSE returns 404), not a library crate, nightly-only (edition 2024, #![feature(likely_unlikely)], cargo-features profile-rustflags, build-std).
Stock Node or browsers: the d8 script notes that stock Node rejects the wide-arithmetic opcodes; V8 needs --experimental-wasm-wide-arithmetic and wasmtime needs -W wide-arithmetic=y (45 or later).

Expecting the loop-invariant speedups for general quotients: the benchmarked loop only produces quotients 0 and 1 (see gotchas), so throughput with a hoisted reciprocal on large quotients is unmeasured.
Other microarchitectures: all numbers come from one macOS laptop with an Intel Core i9-9880H; no aarch64 or newer x86 runs are reported.

integration.dependencies: kernels use only core/std; the benchmark harness pulls criterion 0.8.2, rand 0.10.1, getrandom 0.4.2, num-traits 0.2.19
integration.min_toolchain: Rust nightly (rust-toolchain.toml channel nightly; report used rustc 1.98.0-nightly 2026-06-06) with rust-src and wasm32-wasip1; d8 15.1.52 with --experimental-wasm-wide-arithmetic; wasmtime 45.0.1
integration.platforms: native x86_64 (built with -C target-cpu=native) and wasm32-wasip1 with +wide-arithmetic,+multivalue,+bulk-memory,+reference-types; other targets not tested
integration.thread_safety: pure functions over values with a read-only 512-byte static table; no shared mutable state
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: udiv128/urem128/sdiv128 etc. take and return u128/i128 with the operators' semantics (panics on divide by zero and on i128::MIN / -1), but they live in a binary crate, are unlicensed, and only beat the operator on Wasm when the divisor is loop-invariant and recip128 is hoisted by hand

gotchas: Harness flaw in the headline loop-invariant bench: the divisor is the dividend's own high word with the top bit cleared, and the dividends only flip its low 13 bits (i < 5,000). Reproducing the seeded operands (rand 0.10.1 Xoshiro128PlusPlus::seed_from_u64(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15), checked against rand's own seed_from_u64(0) test vector) gives d_hi = 0x59a28c5de09aec48: 3,144 of 5,000 iterations (62.9%) have quotient 0 and leave the reciprocal path through its Y > X shortcut with no multiply, and the other 1,856 have quotient 1.

On Wasm the builtin __udivti3 is compiler-builtins' trifecta algorithm (selected for target_family wasm in the current rust-lang/rust source), whose div_lz <= duo_lz branch returns quotient 0 or 1 after one compare; divisor and every dividend here have one leading zero, so every builtin iteration takes that early-out (5.93 ns per iteration on d8 vs 18.27 ns for a single general udivrem128, derived from page data). The -38.5% (d8) and -73.4% (wasmtime) therefore compare libcall overhead on a trivial quotient against a mostly-shortcut inlined kernel, not hoisted-reciprocal division on real quotients.

Native -92.8%: on x86_64 compiler-builtins (with its arch feature) uses the asymmetric algorithm, which issues a hardware 128/64 DIV for any divisor with a nonzero high word and has no quotient-0/1 early-out; the native builtin costs 26.9 ns per loop iteration, the same as its single-op cost (26.7 to 27.9 ns), versus 1.95 ns for the reciprocal path (derived from page data).

Single-op benches time one fixed operand pair shared by all six ops: unsigned quotient 9 (3-by-2 kernel, shift 3) and signed |quotient| 1 (negative dividend, positive divisor); the 2-by-1 path for 64-bit divisors is never benchmarked.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No sibling covers 128-bit division: long.js gives a Wasm fast path for 64-bit multiply/divide from JavaScript and galois does finite-field arithmetic in AssemblyScript, so use this only as the reference when you need 128-bit divide in Rust-to-Wasm or are arguing for engine support.
verified_claims_summary: Criterion slope estimates (300 samples, 3 s) on an Intel Core i9-9880H under macOS 15.7.7, rustc 1.98.0-nightly opt-level 3 with fat LTO: with the reciprocal hoisted out of a 5,000-iteration loop, the reciprocal path took 18.24 vs 29.67 us under d8 15.1.52, 13.97 vs 52.51 us under wasmtime 45.0.1 and 9.73 vs 134.44 us natively against Rust's u128 operators, but that loop only produces quotients 0 and 1; single general divisions favour the builtin on V8 (18.27 vs 24.38 ns for udivrem128), tie on wasmtime, and favour the reciprocal natively (17.18 vs 27.86 ns).
status_note: Active research repo (39 commits, last 2026-06-09, report regenerated in that commit) but unlicensed with 0 stars, so reference only; its loop-invariant headline was measured on a degenerate quotient-0-or-1 workload where 62.9% of iterations skip the division entirely and the Wasm builtin takes its own early-out, so the hoisting benefit for general quotients is unproven.
